prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "SOUTHERN COPPER CORP/" (ticker SCCO), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "SCCO", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Southern Copper Corporation

mission.plain: Mine and process copper and other metals at the lowest possible cost while growing production responsibly.

about.plain: Southern Copper digs copper out of huge open-pit mines in Mexico and Peru. It crushes the rock, melts and cleans the copper, and sells the metal to factories around the world. It also gets molybdenum, silver and zinc from the same rock. It is mostly owned by Grupo Mexico, a big Mexican company.
about.customers: Metal traders, smelters, wire and cable makers and other industrial companies in Asia, Europe and the Americas.
about.everyday: The copper in the wires of your house, your phone charger and electric cars may well have come from a mine like Southern Copper's.

money.plain: a metal used to make steel stronger
silver recovered from copper and zinc ore
zinc from its Mexican underground mines

money.part: New Peruvian and Mexican copper projects
money.plain: Tia Maria, Los Chancas, Michiquillay and El Pilar mines aiming to lift copper output toward 1.6 million tons by 2033

result.summary: Southern Copper's advantage is its resource base: it says it has the largest copper reserves in the world, and its big, long-lived Mexican and Peruvian ore bodies with heavy by-product credits make it one of the lowest-cost producers (cash cost net of by-products was $0.58/lb in 2025 and slightly negative in the first half of 2026). That gives it very high margins through the cycle (operating margin 52% in 2025), but it sells a commodity at market prices, so it has no pricing power and its profits swing with copper.

pricingPower.evidence: Copper is sold at LME/COMEX-linked prices; 2025 net sales rose 17.4% to $13,420.0m mainly because the average LME copper price rose 8.7% and silver 41.6% while copper sales volume fell 0.1%, showing revenue follows market prices rather than company-set prices.

moats.evidence: Copper cathode is a standardized commodity; buyers do not pay more for Southern Copper's brand.
Customers can buy LME-grade copper from any producer or trader at market price.
More customers do not make its copper more valuable to other customers.

Operating cash cost net of by-product credits was $0.58/lb in 2025 and -$0.03/lb in the first half of 2026 versus an average LME price of $4.51/lb and $5.94/lb, giving a 2025 operating margin of 52.2%.
Large integrated mine-smelter-refinery complexes in Sonora (Mexico) and southern Peru take decades and billions of dollars to replicate, limiting new entrants nearby.
Its business model is conventional mining; rivals are not held back from copying it.
Long experience running integrated SX-EW, smelting and refining keeps costs low, but the techniques are industry standard.

The company says it believes it has the largest copper reserves in the world, from mines such as Buenavista, La Caridad, Toquepala and Cuajone, plus undeveloped deposits such as Los Chancas and Michiquillay.

customers.evidence: Sales are made under annual contracts and spot sales to traders and fabricators; there is no NPS or loyalty data, and customers buy on price and quality specification rather than loyalty.

talent.evidence: It employed 16,617 people plus about 12,400 contractors at end-2025; it is not on major employer rankings, and Mexican operations have had a history of union disputes.

product.evidence: Its LME-registered cathodes meet the standard grade, but copper is a commodity, so no producer's metal is best in class.

competitors.name: Freeport-McMoRan
competitors.note: Large listed copper-molybdenum producer in the Americas (Peru's Cerro Verde, Arizona) and Indonesia.

competitors.name: Codelco
competitors.note: Chilean state copper giant; competes for the same copper cathode and concentrate buyers.

competitors.name: BHP Group
competitors.note: Owns Escondida in Chile and copper assets in Peru (Antamina stake) and Australia.

competitors.name: Glencore
competitors.note: Copper, zinc and trading; holds Antamina stake in Peru and other copper assets.

competitors.name: Anglo American
competitors.note: Copper in Chile and Peru (Quellaveco near SCC's Peruvian mines); agreed merger with Teck to form Anglo Teck.

competitors.name: Teck Resources
competitors.note: Copper and zinc producer in Chile, Peru (Antamina) and Canada; merging with Anglo American.

competitors.name: Zijin Mining
competitors.note: Fast-growing Chinese copper, gold and zinc miner.

competitors.name: MMG
competitors.note: Owns Las Bambas copper mine in Peru.

competitors.name: First Quantum Minerals
competitors.note: Copper producer in Zambia and Panama.

competitors.name: Rio Tinto
competitors.note: Copper from Escondida stake, Kennecott and Oyu Tolgoi.

competitors.name: KGHM Polska Miedz
competitors.note: Copper and silver miner in Poland and the Americas.

competitors.name: Hudbay Minerals
competitors.note: Smaller copper producer with the Constancia mine in Peru.

competitors.name: Ivanhoe Mines
competitors.note: Kamoa-Kakula copper in the DRC; new low-cost copper supply.

marketShare.measure: tonnes of copper mined (company production / USGS world mine production of 23,000 thousand t)

threats: A fall in copper, silver or molybdenum prices, which drive almost all of its revenue changes
Community and political opposition in Peru (Tia Maria was delayed for years) and Mexico's 2023 mining law changes on concessions and water
Execution risk and cost overruns on a capital program it says exceeds $20.5 billion this decade
Copper substitution by aluminium if prices stay high, and new low-cost supply from DRC and Chinese-backed miners
Controlling shareholder Grupo Mexico (88.9%) leaves minority holders little influence; leadership transition after CEO Oscar Gonzalez Rocha died in April 2026
Environmental liabilities such as the 2014 Buenavista del Cobre spill in Sonora

ceo.name: Leonardo Contreras Lerdo de Tejada
ceo.background: Industrial engineering degree (Universidad Anahuac); director of Grupo Mexico and of Southern Copper; appointed CEO on April 23, 2026 after the death of Oscar Gonzalez Rocha

c1.evidence: Copper mining is a mature, cyclical industry; SCC's mined copper output fell from 973,851 t in 2024 to 956,270 t in 2025, though it is among the largest producers.

c2.evidence: Buyers choose it on price and availability, not loyalty; its lasting edge is low cost from what it says are the world's largest copper reserves, which is hard to copy.

c3.evidence: Ordinary consumers rarely know the name; it is a commodity supplier, not a household brand.

c4.evidence: It publishes no widely known mission statement and communicates mostly about production, costs, projects and dividends.

c6.evidence: “low-cost, copper-rich, Grupo Mexico-controlled” comes to mind for investors; the impression is mixed, positive on assets and dividends but marked by community conflicts in Peru and environmental controversy in Mexico.

c7.evidence: Copper demand is helped by electrification, grids, EVs and data centres, but world mine output was flat at about 23,000 thousand tonnes in 2024 and 2025 according to USGS.

c8.evidence: Growth is mainly more copper from new mines (Tia Maria 120,000 t/yr from 2H27, Los Chancas, Michiquillay, El Pilar) toward 1.6 million tons by 2033, not new markets.

m1.evidence: CEO Leonardo Contreras Lerdo de Tejada was appointed only in April 2026 and has not yet set out a distinct long-term vision publicly.

m2.evidence: He is not a founder; the company is controlled by Grupo Mexico (88.9% ownership at end-2025).

m4.evidence: There is no clear public evidence either way on a servant-leadership style for the new CEO.

m5.evidence: The culture is focused on cost control and mine expansion, not on inventing new products.

m6.evidence: He holds an industrial engineering degree, but his public record is mainly as a Grupo Mexico board member rather than an operator.

m7.evidence: Too early to judge the new CEO's stewardship; the group has faced criticism over the 2014 Sonora spill and Peruvian community conflicts.

m7b.evidence: No record found of a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: He keeps a low public profile.

m9.evidence: He has led the company only since April 2026; first-half 2026 results (net income $3,246.8m vs $1,919.4m) mostly reflect copper prices and the prior team's work.

m10.evidence: The company runs lean on overhead (SG&A $137.8m on $13,420.0m sales in 2025, about 1%), but there is no famous frugality culture.

c10.evidence: Its copper goes into power grids, buildings, electronics and vehicles used worldwide, but indirectly as a raw material.

p2.evidence: Building and running giant open-pit mines and smelters is capital-intensive and important for electrification, but the technology is well known.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 39.1% in 2020 to 52.2% in 2025, but not steadily (55.5% in 2021, 42.4% in 2023).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 debt of $7,994.4m was slightly above cash and short-term investments of $7,329.9m, but 2025 operating cash flow was $4,752.1m and equity was positive at $12,708.6m.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $3,120.7m (2020) to $7,001.7m (2025) and operating cash flow from $2,783.6m to $4,752.1m, but both fell in 2022.

v1.evidence: Copper is a standardized commodity; its edge is low cost, not a better product.

v2.evidence: It does not appear in major best-employer rankings such as Glassdoor or Fortune lists.

c5.evidence: If it disappeared, copper buyers and the economies of Peru and Mexico would notice a loss of about 4% of world mine supply and higher prices, but other miners would partly fill the gap.
